headline: Wootzano's accuracy claim rests on stem detection and clean snips across endless near-identical conveyor frames, so the win is curating which frames to label and proving snip accuracy per crop, not labelling more.
what_they_build: Wootzano sells Avarai, a collaborative robotic packing cell for post-harvest fresh produce, with a food-safe dexterous hand using patented electronic skin and a vision system that detects stems, estimates weight and snips vine produce to a retailer's target weight. Buyers are packhouses and growers, paid for on a per-line ROI case (up to 50% less human labour, 30% cost saving per line). Robots are installed on site, so models must hold up across customer sites, lighting, crops and seasons.
inferred_pipeline: Cameras (guess: Intel RealSense RGB-D, given the stated Intel partnership) capture close-up frames of trusses and punnets on the conveyor at each installed cell.
Guess: frames are recorded locally per site, then shipped or synced to central storage; unclear whether all sites stream back or only on-request clips during commissioning.
Engineers select clips by hand around failures (missed stem, bad snip, bruising, dropped fruit) and label stems, fruit and snip points in an open-source or in-house tool (guess: CVAT or similar).
Detection / segmentation and weight-estimation models are retrained centrally, validated on a held-out set, then pushed to cells.
Guess: field performance is judged by packhouse throughput and reject rates rather than per-class mAP, so model regressions per crop variety are hard to see before rollout.
Tactile e-skin data is likely handled in a separate stream from vision, with no shared record of what happened in a given grasp.

hypotheses.pain: Near-duplicate conveyor frames dominate. Labelling budget goes on the thousandth ordinary truss while rare failure modes (tangled vines, occluded stems, soft or damaged fruit) stay under-represented.
hypotheses.evidence: A fixed-camera cell running a full packhouse shift produces highly repetitive imagery; the site sells consistency ("a clean, precise snip, each and every time").
hypotheses.encord_answer: Index registers frames in their own bucket, computes embeddings and quality metrics, and lets them de-duplicate and diversity-sample into Collections. Our own warehouse-stream test cut frames to label by 61% while keeping 95% of racks, and the curated pick beat a random pick of equal size.

hypotheses.pain: Each new site, crop variety or season is a cold start. Labelling a fresh set by hand delays go-live, which conflicts with the "Day 1 install, Day 2 ready" promise.
hypotheses.evidence: Site promises next-day readiness and adaptability across produce; a deployed-robot business inevitably faces per-packhouse lighting, punnet and variety drift.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Agents run their existing detector as a pre-labelling stage in the workflow, so a new site's data arrives part-labelled and humans only correct. Annotate adds SAM 3 auto-segmentation, object tracking and interpolation on native video for fruit and truss masks.

hypotheses.pain: No clear way to prove which data fixes a snip failure. Model changes are judged by packhouse throughput after rollout, which is slow and expensive feedback.
hypotheses.evidence: Marketing quantifies line productivity, not model metrics; no ML or CV job ads found, suggesting a small team with no dedicated data or evaluation tooling.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Active imports their predictions for mAP/mAR/F1, PR curves and confusion matrix, sliced by class, IoU threshold and any data metric (for example blur or occlusion). Metric-to-failure correlation names which frames to label next, and label validation surfaces stem labels that are simply wrong.

ontology.name: Vine / truss stem
ontology.why: Stem geometry drives the snip; a centreline is more useful than a box

ontology.name: Snip point
ontology.why: The exact cut location the controller needs, evaluated as pixel error

ontology.name: Individual fruit
ontology.why: Per-fruit area feeds weight estimation to the retailer's target

ontology.name: Grasp point on fruit
ontology.why: Links vision to the e-skin force decision for the dexterous hand

ontology.name: Punnet / tray
ontology.why: Placement and fill checks against retailer packing spec

ontology.name: Defect or damage (bruise, split, mould)
ontology.why: Reject decisions and evidence that handling caused no bruising

ontology.name: Occlusion / tangled truss
ontology.why: Flags the hard frames worth over-sampling in training

ontology.name: Crop variety and site conditions
ontology.why: Lets them slice model performance per packhouse, variety and shift

case_study.name: Automotus
case_study.why_it_matches: Fixed cameras producing huge volumes of repetitive street footage, same problem as a fixed cell over a conveyor: the constraint is choosing which frames deserve labels, not annotation speed alone.
case_study.numbers: +20% mAP, 35% smaller dataset, 33% lower labelling cost after curating with Encord.

proof_of_value: Week 1, day 1-2: register one packhouse's recorded footage from their own S3/GCS bucket in Index (data never moves), generate embeddings and quality metrics, show the duplicate clusters and the blurred or badly lit tail.

Week 1, day 3-5: build two Collections of equal size from the same footage, one random and one de-duplicated plus diversity-sampled. Success metric: at least 40% fewer frames needed to cover the same set of distinct trusses and punnets.

Week 2, day 1-2: set up the stem polyline, snip keypoint, fruit bitmask and defect ontology in Annotate with SAM 3 and object tracking on native video; measure minutes per truss versus their current tool.

Week 2, day 3-4: if they can share a model, run it as an Agent pre-labelling stage and import predictions into Active. Success metric: percentage of pre-labels accepted without edit, plus a confusion matrix and per-slice F1 on stem detection.

Week 2, day 5: train or fine-tune on the curated Collection versus the random one of equal size. Success metric: higher snip-point accuracy and stem F1 on a held-out packhouse, and a ranked list of the next 500 frames to label.
discovery_questions: When you commission a new packhouse or a new variety, how many frames do you label before the cell is ready, and who does that labelling?
How do you currently decide which recorded frames are worth annotating, and how much of what you label turns out to be near-duplicate?
What does a snip failure look like in your logs, and how do you trace it back to the training data that caused it?
Do you evaluate stem detection and weight estimation per site and per variety, or only by line throughput after rollout?
Does footage stay on site in each packhouse, or does it come back to your own cloud storage, and what have customers said about data leaving their premises?
risks: Small, hardware-led team with no CV or ML job ads open, so labelling may be handled informally in-house with CVAT and seen as free.
Robotics capital spend may leave no budget line for data tooling; the buying case has to be framed as commissioning time per new site.
Packhouse customers may forbid footage leaving their site, which limits what can be centralised (Encord's bucket-registration model helps, but needs checking early).
Evidence base is thin: no recent signals, no job ads, and our understanding of their crops, sensors and volumes is largely inference.
